questions.q: In `lsblk` output, what does it mean when a partition like `sdb1` has no value in the MOUNTPOINT column?
options: The partition is corrupted and cannot be used
The partition exists but isn't currently attached to any directory in the filesystem tree
The partition is the root filesystem
lsblk cannot detect that partition's filesystem
questions.explain: A blank MOUNTPOINT means the partition has a filesystem but hasn't been mounted anywhere yet, so it isn't accessible through any directory.

questions.q: What must be true before running `sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /data` will succeed?
options: /dev/sdb1 must already be mounted somewhere else
The /data directory must already exist as the mount point
/etc/fstab must already contain an entry for /dev/sdb1
The system must be rebooted first
questions.explain: mount attaches a filesystem to an existing directory (the mount point). If /data doesn't exist, it needs to be created first with mkdir.

questions.q: Why does `/etc/fstab` typically reference a filesystem by its UUID rather than a device name like `/dev/sdb1`?
options: UUIDs are shorter and easier to type
Device names like /dev/sdb1 can shift if a disk is added or removed, while a UUID stays the same regardless
Device names are not supported in /etc/fstab at all
UUIDs are required by the ext4 filesystem specifically
questions.explain: Device names depend on detection order at boot and can change if storage is added or removed. A filesystem's UUID is fixed and unaffected by such changes, making fstab entries more reliable.

questions.q: Why run `sudo mount -a` after editing `/etc/fstab`, rather than just rebooting to test it?
options: mount -a is required to save the file to disk
mount -a mounts any fstab entries not already mounted and surfaces syntax errors immediately, without risking a failed boot
mount -a permanently deletes incorrect fstab entries
There's no reason — rebooting is always safer
questions.explain: mount -a attempts to mount everything listed in fstab that isn't already mounted. Running it immediately after an edit catches typos or bad UUIDs right away, rather than discovering them during a reboot when the system might fail to come up cleanly.

questions.q: What does `df -h /data` show after `/dev/sdb1` has been mounted at `/data`?
options: The contents of every file under /data
The size, used space, available space, and use percentage of the filesystem mounted at /data
The UUID of /dev/sdb1
A list of every process currently reading from /data
questions.explain: df -h reports disk space usage in human-readable units for the filesystem containing the given path — confirming the mount succeeded and showing its capacity.
